title: The First Computers
objective: After this level you can describe Babbage's engines, Ada Lovelace and the first electronic computers.
summary: Babbage designed mechanical computers; Lovelace wrote an early program. The ABC, Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different rule.

cards.headline: A computer Babbage designed by 1849 was finally built in 1991.
cards.body: London's Science Museum followed Charles Babbage's plans for Difference Engine No. 2, designed in 1847-1849. The calculating section, finished in 1991, works as he intended. Babbage never saw it. So who built the first computer? That depends on your rules.

cards.headline: Babbage's Analytical Engine
cards.body: In 1834 Babbage conceived something bigger: the Analytical Engine, a mechanical machine to be programmed with punched cards. It had a store to hold numbers and a mill to do the arithmetic. Sound familiar? That's Level 51's memory and processing, sketched in brass and gears. It was never built.

cards.fact: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published what is often called the first computer program.
cards.context: Her notes on the Analytical Engine showed, step by step, how it could compute a series called the Bernoulli numbers. She also saw that it could work on letters and musical notes, not only numbers. A program for a machine that did not exist yet.

cards.headline: Four machines, four kinds of first

events.label: Atanasoff-Berry Computer, Iowa: electronic, but not programmable
Zuse's Z3, Germany: program-controlled, but built from relays, not electronics
Colossus, Bletchley Park: electronic and programmable in a limited way; broke codes and stayed secret for decades
ENIAC, Philadelphia: the first programmable, general-purpose electronic computer

cards.headline: So who was first? First at what?
cards.body: Each machine wins by a different rule: mechanical design, program control, electronics, general purpose. Historians still argue about which rule matters. Even the courts got involved: in 1973 a US court ruled the ENIAC patent invalid, finding its inventors had drawn on John Atanasoff's ideas. The honest answer to "who built the first computer?" is a question back: first at what?

cards.headline: First computers: counted
learned: Babbage's engines were mechanical; one was built in 1991 and works
Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first program (1843)
ABC, Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different rule
Who was first depends on the rule you pick

options.label: Zuse's Z3

questions.prompt: Why is there no single agreed answer to which machine was the first computer?

options.label: All of them were built in the same year
options.rationale: They span 1939 to 1946, plus Babbage a century earlier.

A court banned the question

questions.prompt: Babbage's Analytical Engine had a "store" and a "mill". Which of Level 51's four computer jobs did the mill do?

options.label: Input
options.rationale: Input came in on punched cards.

options.label: Output
options.rationale: The mill worked on numbers rather than showing them.

questions.explanation: The store held numbers (memory); the mill did the arithmetic (processing), like a CPU.
